lesson.title: Organizing Classes into Families
lesson.summary: A class hierarchy arranges related classes into parent-child chains built on inheritance, so that shared behavior lives once in a common ancestor while each subclass overrides only the parts that make it distinct.
lesson.body:
Inheritance lets one class, a child class, take on the attributes and methods of another, its parent class, and then add or override specific pieces. A class hierarchy is what you get when you use that repeatedly: not just one parent and one child, but a whole family tree of related classes, each one more specific than the class above it.

```python
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def speak(self):
        return f"{self.name} makes a sound."

class Dog(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Meow!"

class Puppy(Dog):
    def speak(self):
        return f"{self.name} yips excitedly."

animals = [Animal("Generic"), Dog("Rex"), Cat("Milo"), Puppy("Biscuit")]
for a in animals:
    print(a.speak())
```

This prints:

Generic makes a sound.
Rex says Woof!
Milo says Meow!
Biscuit yips excitedly.

Every one of these objects has a name attribute and a speak() method, both ultimately defined by Animal, but each class in the hierarchy overrides speak() with something more specific to itself. Puppy inherits from Dog, which inherits from Animal, making this a three-level hierarchy rather than just one parent and one child. Puppy never mentions name at all, it does not need to, since __init__ comes from Animal two levels up, and Puppy has no reason to override something that already does exactly what it needs.

The reason to organize classes this way, rather than writing four unrelated classes that each redefine everything from scratch, is that shared behavior only needs to be written once, in the common ancestor, while each subclass focuses only on what actually makes it different. If ten more animal types were added to this hierarchy, none of them would need to reimplement __init__ or reinvent what name means, they would only need to override speak() if their sound is genuinely different, and could simply omit speak() entirely if Animal's generic version happens to be good enough.

A hierarchy also gives you a reliable way to ask what something is, using the built-in isinstance() function, which checks whether an object belongs to a given class or any of that class's ancestors.

```python
print(isinstance(animals[3], Dog))
print(isinstance(animals[3], Animal))
print(isinstance(animals[1], Puppy))
```

This prints True, True, False. animals[3] is the Puppy, and a Puppy is a Dog (it inherits from Dog directly) and is also an Animal (it inherits from Dog, which inherits from Animal, so the relationship carries up the whole chain). animals[1] is Rex, a plain Dog, and a Dog is not automatically a Puppy just because Puppy happens to be one particular kind of Dog, inheritance only flows downward in the sense that a subclass gains everything from its ancestors, not the other way around.

This "is-a" relationship, a Puppy is a Dog, a Dog is an Animal, is the defining idea behind when inheritance is the right tool. It should describe a real specialization, not just two classes that happen to share some fields. Designing a good hierarchy means finding the genuinely shared behavior and pulling it up into a common ancestor, while keeping what varies down in the specific subclasses, which is exactly the shape you can see in how little code Puppy needed to write to become a fully working class.
